A walk is easy to measure. Your phone counts steps, and it can turn the steps into distance. When you push a cart, or when the wind blows against you, the numbers can be a little off. People use these numbers to see whether they are close to a goal, like ten thousand steps a day. They ask, how many steps have I taken, or, how far did I go. If the number looks wrong, they say, that is not correct, I walked more than that, or, reset my steps for today. Some people also say, set my goal to eight thousand, to make it easier.

Homework is work for school that you do at home. Every subject has its own assignments, and each one has a due date. Students write them on a board, in a notebook, or on a phone. A short break helps the brain, and people often say, remind me to study for twenty minutes, then rest. When a due date moves, they say, change the math test to Friday, or, put the essay on Thursday. They also say, what homework do I have tonight? After a spicy lunch they might say, give me five more minutes. The right words help a student plan the week.

Gus the gardener wiped his forehead. It was a hot afternoon, and he wanted to drive to the garden center before it closed. He put on his sunglasses and said to his phone, How long to the garden center on Elm Street? The assistant understood that he wanted the drive time. It checked the traffic and said he would arrive in twenty-five minutes. Gus asked for the quickest way, and the assistant said to take the river road. It started the directions and read them out loud one turn at a time. Gus drove with the window open and came to the garden center ten minutes before closing.

Meal planning means deciding what to eat before you are hungry. Many families go through the week day by day: pasta on Monday, soup on Tuesday, and so on. A plan also helps with shopping, since you only buy what you need, like one ounce of cheese for each sandwich. People change the plan with simple words. They say, swap Tuesday and Wednesday, or, no meat on Friday, or, make dinner for six this week. Sometimes they ask, what can I make with eggs and rice? If they go out, they say, skip tonight, we are eating at a restaurant.

Lily was eight, and she was sitting at the kitchen table with her mom's tablet. She had a picture of a toy motorcycle in her head, a deep blue one. She said to the assistant, Find a blue toy motorcycle and print a picture of it for my wish list. The assistant understood two things: she wanted to see toy motorcycles for sale and she wanted a printed picture. It showed her three toys, and she pointed to the deep blue one. The assistant sent the picture to the printer, and a page came out. Lily taped it to the fridge, and her mom smiled when she saw it.

Someone wants to know if the water is warm enough to swim.
Is the sea warm?
Water temperature?
How cold is it in the waves today?
Can I swim without a wetsuit?
My cousin is on the sofa at home and wants to know if the sea is nice for the kids.
I paid for two beach chairs, so tell me if it is worth getting in the water.
Would I be too cold if I jumped in now?
Could I ask you how warm the ocean is right now?
Should I bring a towel for a quick dip or a full swim?

Every cup of coffee or tea can be changed to fit the person drinking it. Most people have a usual order, but a temporary change is easy too. Someone tired might ask for a stronger coffee. Someone else says, make it sweeter, or, just one sugar please. A smoothie can be thicker with less ice or thinner with more milk. When a friend jokes that black coffee tastes burnt, everyone laughs, and then they ask for milk. Short words work best: stronger, weaker, sweeter, less sugar, no ice. A coffee machine or a drink app listens for these words and changes only that one cup. To keep a change, say keep it as my usual, and it stays like a note in your pocket.

Mr. Osei runs a small shop, and last month's electric bill was high. Between customers he typed on his phone: how much powr did the shop use today. The assistant understood that he wanted today's electricity use. It checked the meter and said the shop had used forty-two units since midnight, which was more than usual. Most of it came from the big freezer at the back. Mr. Osei remembered that a delivery truck had been loading all morning with the shop door open. He asked the assistant to filter the list so it showed only the freezer, and the assistant did. The line was shallow at night and tall in the afternoon. Then he said, remind me to check the door seal. The assistant set a reminder for six that evening.

When you order food from an app, you pick the dishes, check the address, and press a button. The restaurant gets a message and starts cooking. A courier takes the bag and carries it to your door, sometimes with one arm on the handlebars and the other holding the bag. The app shows how long the trip will take. People change a few things: the tip, the delivery time, and the notes for the kitchen. They might say, put a bigger tip, make it arrive by seven, or no onions please. If the food is late, you can ask where it is. A black bag keeps meals warm on the road. Most apps let you say these things in plain words, and the order changes before the kitchen starts.

Lena had just moved to the city and knew almost nobody. A neighbour invited her to a monthly game night, and her budget was small, so she wanted to bring the cards she already owned. In the lift she typed in a hurry: how do i shufle a deck for rummy. The assistant understood that she wanted two things: how to shuffle well and how to start a game of rummy. It explained that she should split the deck into two halves, let the corners fall together, and do it three times. Then it read out the rules in short steps: deal ten cards to each player, turn one card face up, and make sets. Lena practised in the lift until she reached the right floor.

Mrs. Patel was a retired teacher who still loved numbers. One afternoon she was making a big pot of soup for her club, and every ingredient was written for four people. She needed it for twenty-five. She asked the kitchen speaker, what is twenty-five times three. The assistant understood that she wanted two numbers multiplied, and it told her the answer was seventy-five. Mrs. Patel had guessed seventy, so she laughed and said she was close. Next she asked, what is half of seventy-five, and the assistant said thirty-seven and a half. She wrote both numbers on the back of an envelope and began to measure the carrots.

Walter was not good with technology, but his granddaughter had put a quiz app on his tablet. He wanted to play it on the train, where there is no signal, and he worried it would not work offline. He held the tablet and said slowly, can I play the quiz without the internet, and remind me tomorrow at seven to practise. The assistant understood both parts. It said the quiz worked offline once the questions were saved, and it saved the next episode of questions to the tablet. Then it set a reminder for tomorrow at seven in the morning. Walter smiled, put the tablet down, and went to brush his teeth, feeling that he could do this after all.

Dana was late for work, and the kitchen floor was a serious mess after breakfast. She grabbed her bag and said to her phone, start the robot vacuum for twenty-five minutes. The assistant understood that she wanted the vacuum to run in the kitchen and stop after that time. It sent the command to the robot, and a small light came on. The robot's camera looked around and found the table legs. It even went around a slice of toast on the floor, and then it told the phone it could not pick it up. Dana laughed, said thanks, and locked the door. When she came home, the floor was clean and the robot was back on its dock.

Nora came home after a long night shift at the hospital, still in her blue shirt. She was too tired to type, so she said to her phone, post the photo from the ward party and make it temporary, gone after twenty-four hours. The assistant understood that she wanted to share one photo as a story that disappears. It found the newest photo from the party, and the picture took a moment to load. Then it asked which friends should see it, and Nora said just close friends. The assistant posted it for close friends only and said it would vanish tomorrow morning. Nora smiled, set her phone on the table, and went to bed.

name: scale_recipe
does: A tool that changes the amounts in a recipe so it feeds more or fewer people.
inputs: the recipe, how many people it makes now, and how many people you want to feed
people say:
- Make this soup for eight instead of four.
- I only have a small home pan, so cut it in half.
- I have to crack six eggs for a big batch, so how much flour is that?
- Double the cake for my sister's party.
- Can you shrink these amounts for one person?
- My cookbook says six servings but we are two.

The router is the small box that brings the internet into your home. It sends wifi through the air so phones, laptops and televisions can connect without wires. Every network has a name and a password. When guests visit, they ask for the password and cheer when the video loads. If the connection is slow, people say, restart the router, or, move the box closer to the living room. Some routers have a guest network, so visitors can get online without seeing your other devices. People also change the password now and then, and the last time you did it, you probably wrote it down. A good router may cost about sixty dollars, and it can last for years.

Kai was running late for a weekend trip to the hills and had only a minute. He typed on his phone: whats the wether on the ridge sat morning. The assistant understood that he wanted the forecast for the ridge on Saturday morning. It said there would be light rain until ten, then clear skies, and the trail would be safe if he left after lunch. It added that more rain would touch the ridge by evening, so he should come down early. Kai asked it to make a packing list. The assistant wrote down a rain jacket, boots, water, a map, and a pen for his notebook. Kai grabbed his pack and ran out the door.

Ms. Green owned a shop that sold fresh peas and beans, and on Monday her laptop screen went black. She was worried. She said to the speaker beside it, I would be very grateful if you could help me, because my customers are waiting and I must print the order sheet from the main folder. The assistant understood that she needed the laptop to wake up and the order sheet opened. It said the battery was empty, so it asked her to plug in the cable. After a minute the screen lit up, and the assistant opened the main folder and found the order sheet. A fly landed on the keyboard, and Ms. Green waved it away and pressed print.

A game timer helps everyone play fairly. In a board game, each player may get a minute to think, and a message pops up or a bell rings when time is up. Timers are also used in word puzzles, where the time limit is narrow and the fun is in the rush. People change the timer all the time. They say, make it two minutes, or, give me thirty more seconds. If the game is paused, you can lift the lid of the box and count the pieces while the clock waits. Say start, pause, reset or stop, and the timer follows. A scoreboard works the same way: people say, give Sam two points, or, take one back.

Someone wants to know how far they walked today.
How far today?
how far did i walk todya
Distance so far?
I listened to a whole album while out, so how many miles was that?
Can you convert my steps into kilometres?
It was a difficult hill, so I want to see how much ground I covered.
What's my total for the walk?
Could you tell me how much distance I've done since breakfast?
Please tell me how far I went, because I want to know if I reached my goal.

Ana was hosting a game afternoon for her kids, and her hands were full of juice boxes. She said to the speaker, start a ten minute timer for the card game. The assistant understood and started a ten minute timer. Then Ana said, no wait, make it fifteen, the gray cards are harder. The assistant changed the timer to fifteen minutes and said the new time out loud. Ana also asked it to forward the game rules to her husband, because he was coming home early. The assistant sent the rules to him as a message. Her daughter put a paper flower on the table as the prize. The kids cheered, and the timer kept counting.

When you write on a phone or computer, there are small tools that help. Spelling checks underline words that look wrong. A word count tells you how long the text is, and some assignments have a maximum, like five hundred words. If you cannot type, you can talk and let the writing app listen. Some phones have a sensor that notices your voice, and if the microphone is muted, you can say, unmute the mic. People use easy words to change a draft: shorter, longer, fix the spelling, make it more polite. Editing means reading it again and changing a few lines. You can ask for a copy before you change anything, so the first draft is still there.

Watering is the most common job in a garden. Plants need water to grow, but not too much. A sprinkler can do it for you on a timer, so the water continues for ten minutes every morning. People change how long it runs and when it starts. They say, water the beans for longer, or, skip tomorrow, it's going to rain. Seeds are kept dry in a jar until spring. Soil should feel smooth and a little damp, not like mud. When the sun is strong, people water early or late in the day. A garden app can look at the weather and say when to start, stop or wait. You only have to tell it what you want in plain words.

Mr. Hall was a retired teacher with a new robot mower and a neat lawn. At breakfast he said to the speaker, mow the lawn at nine. The assistant understood and scheduled the mower for nine. A minute later Mr. Hall remembered his trip to the pharmacy. No, he said, make it ten, I'll be out at nine. The assistant moved the job to ten and told him the new time. He also asked it to skip the edges, because wet leaves had started to fall and could jam the blades. The assistant changed the plan so the mower would cut only the middle of the grass. Mr. Hall nodded, took his coat, and walked to the pharmacy.

name: share_photo_album
does: Sends a photo album to the people you choose.
inputs: the album name and who should get it
people say:
- Send my class trip pictures to Mum.
- I want everyone to know how the party went, so share those photos.
- Let Grandpa see the beach album.
- Mail the most recent pictures to my sister.
- Can the whole family look at the holiday photos?

name: check_front_door
does: Looks at the front door camera and tells you if someone is there or if the door is locked.
inputs: which door to check
people say:
- Is anyone at the door?
- I'm making noodles, can you see who rang the bell?
- Did I lock up?
- Let me talk to the person outside.
- Show me my favorite camera, the one by the porch.
- Is the back door closed?

Rosa worked as a gardener and had a bad cold. While her hands were in the soil, she said to her phone, remind me to take my medicine at eight. The assistant understood and made a reminder for eight. Rosa then said, no, nine, I want to eat first. The assistant changed the reminder to nine and said so. She also asked it to boost the volume of the alarm, because her daughter had borrowed the phone and turned the sound down. The assistant raised the volume. It added that the label said to take the pill with water and to rest for a few days. Rosa nodded and kept planting.

name: start_nap_timer
does: Starts a timer for the baby's nap and tells you when it is time to wake them.
inputs: how long the nap should be
people say:
- The baby just went down, tell me in an hour.
- I'm far away in the garden, so ring the remote speaker when the nap is over.
- She will fall asleep soon, so please start a nap clock.
- Wake me in forty minutes, I'll keep the house quiet.
- How long has he been sleeping?

Person: Can you start a workout for me?
Assistant: Sure. How many minutes do you have?
Person: Thirty minutes, please. I want to run by the lake.
Assistant: I can start a thirty minute run and keep the time.
Person: Actually, make it twenty. I have to pick up the kids at four.
Assistant: Okay, twenty minutes. Should I play your favourite playlist?

A can of pens on a desk is a good start, but most writing today happens on screens. A draft is the first version of a text. It does not need to be perfect. After that you read it again and fix the spelling, change some words, and make it shorter or longer. A word count tells you how many words you have so far, which is useful when a teacher wants a certain length. When you have been typing for hours your eyes can feel sore, so people take breaks. A writing app can notify you when you reach your goal. Say, count my words, or, read it back to me, and the app will do it.

A post is a picture or a few words that you share with friends online. People can like it, which means they pressed a small button to show they enjoyed it, and they can follow you to see your next posts. Each time something happens, a notification may pop up. If the buzzing is too much, people say, keep notifications calm, or, only tell me about messages. A post that gets a lot of attention might double its likes in a day. When a quarter of your friends have liked a picture, you may feel proud. You can also say, hide this post, or, delete my last picture, and the app will do it.

An oven cooks food with heat, and you choose how hot it gets and for how long. The setting is a number, like one hundred and eighty degrees. A kettle boils water and clicks off by itself. A coffee machine can make a small or a large cup. People ask for changes in simple words: hotter, cooler, ten more minutes, or, keep it warm. A recipe is a document that tells you the exact time and heat, and you can ask the machine to calculate how long a bigger dish will take. A dishwasher has short and long cycles, so you can say, wash quickly, or, use the strong cycle, when the pots are dirty.

Ana had just moved to the city for a new job. Her desk at the office was bare, and she wanted something tidy. She sat on her bed with her phone.

"Order a desk lamp," she said to the assistant. Then she stopped. "No, I mean a desk organizer. The lamp can wait."

Ana asked how to spell the name of the shop, because she wanted to tell her sister. The assistant spelled it out, letter by letter.

Birthdays are easy to forget, so most people write them down. A calendar app can keep the date and give you a reminder. People change the reminder with words like, tell me a week early, or make it repeat every year. They ask for gift ideas too, such as, what can I give a man who likes fishing? Some people want a card as well, and they say, help me organize cards for all my cousins.

A red mark on the calendar makes a birthday easy to see. If the date changes, you can say, move Dan's birthday to the fourth. If you no longer need it, you can say, remove the reminder.

A notes app is a place to keep ideas so you do not lose them. Some people prefer to type, and others like to speak. A voice note is a short recording that the phone can turn into words. At night a thought can come, and you can say, make a note: buy stamps. Later you can say, find my note about the wifi password, or read me my last note.

The app works well when notes have a short name. People change notes with words like, add milk to the shopping note, or delete the old one. They also say, put this note at the top, when they want to find it fast.

Grandpa Harold had taken a nice walk through the forest park. When he came back to the gate, he could not remember where he had left the car. He took out his phone and spoke to it slowly.

"Tell me where I parked the car. No, wait. I mean tell me where the car is, not where I parked it last week."

The assistant understood that he wanted the place where the car was right now. It looked at the last spot his phone had saved and said that the car was in the second row of the north car park, near the picnic tables. It showed the place on the map.

Harold watched his step and followed the little dot all the way to the car.

Things at home wear out, and a repair is easier when you plan it. A filter in a heater or a fan needs a change every few months. People say, remind me to change the filter every three months. If something breaks, they say, book a plumber for Thursday, and they tell the shop what is wrong, such as the depth of the water under the sink, or where the leak started. Someone with a broken favourite kettle might say, find me a repair shop near home.

A reminder helps you put the job on the calendar. You can change it with words like, make it earlier, or move it to next month.

Walter was not good with technology, but he wanted to write a letter to his neighbour. The neighbour's dog was noisy, and Walter had also borrowed some butter and wanted to say thank you. He sat in front of the screen and spoke in a careful voice.

"Please fix my spelling and tell me how many words are in this letter," he said. He did not know if the assistant would understand.

It did. It fixed three words and said that the letter had forty-two words. It also said it had left the kind parts as they were.

Walter nodded. He read the letter once more, printed it, and walked next door to put it in the mailbox.

Jo was a busy parent, and the children were hungry. Dinner was not ready, and the lawn needed water. A wire fence ran along one side of the garden, and the kids were learning to ride their bikes beside it.

"Run the sprinklers for half the time today," Jo said to the assistant. "It rained a little this morning, so we don't need the full time."

The assistant understood that she wanted the usual time cut in half. The sprinklers normally ran for twenty minutes, so it set them to run for ten. It said plainly that it had made the change for today only and that tomorrow they would go back to twenty minutes.

Jo thanked it and went to make dinner.

"need a parking spot near the school tomorrow at seven"

The assistant understood that she wanted a car park close to the school for the next morning at seven. It found one two streets away with a lot of free spaces and said it opened at half past six. It offered to remind her to leave early.

Mia said yes. She asked the assistant to upload the map of the car park to her phone so that she could find it fast. The assistant saved it, and she put her coins back in her bag.

A scorekeeper is useful for board games, because people forget the numbers. It tells everyone who is winning and when the game is over. Players say things like, start a ten minute timer, add five points for Sam, or undo that, I pressed the wrong one. They also ask, who is winning?

In a game with a ladder, players climb up the board, and the scores can change fast. A family may play downstairs on a rainy day with a melon-shaped timer on the table. When the timer rings, the game stops, and someone says, read me the scores. If the rules are unclear, you can say, what is the rule for ties?

A focus timer helps you work without getting tired. A common way is to work for twenty-five minutes and then rest for five. People say, start a focus timer, make the break longer, or skip this break. A routine is a list of things you do at the same time every day, such as wake up, train, eat breakfast and begin work.

A healthy routine includes short breaks. Some people sit by the fireplace with a cup of tea, and others walk around the block. You can tell your assistant, remind me to stand up every hour, or change my break to ten minutes. If the timer is too short, you can say, make it longer.

Arthur was not good with technology, but he had a newspaper in his lap and a plan for Friday. He wanted to eat out and still sleep well afterwards. He talked to the speaker slowly.

"I can't hear a thing in the loud places," he said. "I would like to eat early on Friday somewhere calm."

The assistant understood that Arthur wanted a quiet restaurant and an early table. It looked for places with good reviews for being calm, and it found a small restaurant by the river that opened at five. It asked if he wanted a table for one, and Arthur said two, because his sister would come.

The assistant booked a table for two at five o'clock on Friday and read the address aloud.

Lena was an office worker, and it was almost noon. Her desk was full of papers, and she had not read the manual for the new lunch app. The phone was the only thing she wanted to talk to.

"Usual lunch," she said.

The assistant understood that she wanted the same lunch she had ordered most days, a chicken salad from the cafe across the road. It said so, and asked if she wanted to change anything. Lena said no, but she wanted the weight of the bag to be small, so that nothing would spill. The assistant put a note on the order.

It said the lunch would come in twenty minutes. Lena went back to her papers and was ready when the bell rang.

Homework is work from school that you finish at home. Each assignment has a subject and a due date. A phone or speaker can keep a list, so you know what is next. Students say things like, add a math test on Friday, what is due next week, or move my essay to Monday.

Some people ask for a reminder the evening before, and others ask for a study timer. A student with a trip to a field for science class might say, remind me to bring my boots. When a job is done, you can say, mark it finished. If a teacher changes the date, you can say, change the due date to Thursday.

I want to send it to my sister, and she will only believe I baked it if she can see the crust up close." The phone understood that Omar wanted a close photo of the loaf. A fraction of a minute later, Lena wrote back with three happy faces. Omar grinned and wiped the flour off his hands.

Priya had just moved to a new city, and her hotel room was almost empty of her things. She had only one bag. She said to her phone, "I need a room for twenty-five nights near the train station. Jonas was a student with a small kitchen and a big appetite. He asked his speaker, "How long do I bake chicken and potatoes together? I want something tasty, but I'm in a hurry." The speaker understood that Jonas wanted one pan of chicken and potatoes, and that he had little time. It told him the total cooking time was about forty minutes at a hot oven. Then it said he could skip peeling the potatoes to save time. Jonas set the oven to the right heat and cut the potatoes into small pieces. The speaker started a timer for twenty-five minutes, then another for the last fifteen. When the food was done, it smelled wonderful.

My daughter's seat belt is loose in my car, so I don't want to drive." It booked a small car, wrote a note to keep the air cool, and told her the driver would arrive in six minutes at the school gate. Dana waved at the kids and waited.

Bread dough needs warmth, time and a little care. When people bake, they follow a recipe, but they also change things. A cold kitchen makes dough rise slowly, and a warm one makes it rise faster. On a cloudy, damp day, dough can feel stickier. Some bakers put a pan of hot water in the oven, a kind of steam bath, so the crust stays crisp. People ask for changes in simple words. They say, "Set a timer for one hour," "Make the oven hotter," or "How long until it's ready?" Most of the time, a cook just wants the dough to be soft and the crust to be golden.

A thermostat keeps a home at the heat people like. You pick a number, and the heating works until the room reaches it, then it stops. A radiator or a small heater may glow or feel hot to the touch. Many people use only a few settings, like warm in the morning and cooler at night. When they want a change, they say, "Make it warmer," "It's freezing in here," or "Turn the heat down to twenty." Some say, "Keep the bedroom cozy tonight." All of these ask for the same kind of thing: a different temperature in a room at a certain time.

A photo is a picture of a moment that you want to keep. Most people take pictures with a phone, and for a while they stay in one place, like an album. People often change a few things. They may crop a photo, make it brighter, or share it with a friendly neighbor or a cousin far away. When people want to chill and look back, they open an album and flip through. Some ask for changes out loud. They say, "Take a picture," "Show me last summer," "Send this to Grandma," or "Make a new album called Trip." Each request is a simple way to take, find or share a photo.

Counting days helps us plan. People ask how many days are left until a birthday, a trip or a holiday. They also ask how old someone will be. A calendar page on the wall, a rug with a number game for kids, or a phone can do the counting. People change the date they are counting to, or they ask the same question for a different day. Some friends even tweet about how many days are left before a party. People say, "How many days until my birthday?", "How old will she be in May?", or "Count the days to the trip." It is a sweet way to look forward to something.

Music is something people use to relax, work or dance. On a speaker or a phone, you can change a few things. You can pick a song or an artist, make a playlist, skip a track you don't like, or turn the volume up and down. Sometimes a song needs a boost, so people ask for more bass. People say, "Play something calm," "Next song," "Turn it up," or "Make a playlist for cooking." If a pan sizzles loudly in the kitchen, they might say, "I can't hear it, make it louder." A clear request helps the speaker find the right song quickly.

The next day, a local mail carrier walked by at eight, and the speaker said, "Someone is at the door." Mr. Harlan waved at the camera and smiled. His bike was safe in the shed too.

Most lights in a home have a simple job: to help you see. A lamp lights a corner, a ceiling light fills a room, and a smart bulb can change its color. Some lights are narrow, like a reading lamp, and others are wide. People change the brightness and the color depending on the time of day. In the evening, a warm yellow light helps them relax. In the morning, they want something bright and white. A puppy might cry in the dark, so the owner leaves a little light on. People say, "Make it brighter," "Dim the lights," "Turn on the lamp," or "Make the bulb blue."

It said to cook the rice for fifteen minutes and then build the sauce in a single pan. Sam smiled and drove home to make dinner.

A storm can cause trouble at home. The wind may knock down a power line, or heavy rain may flood a street. That is why many homes have smoke alarms, flashlights and a radio. They say, "Call for help," "Call the fire station," or "Where is the flashlight?" After the problem is over, they may finish by saying, "Tell my family I am safe." Clear and short words are the best ones.

Vik was a driver who spent his whole day on the road. At the office, he needed to scan an extra copy of his license. He told his phone, "Print two more copies of my driving license, and scan the old one first. I have half a stack of paper left, so use only one page for both sides." The phone understood that Vik wanted one scan and two copies on a single page. It checked the printer and said there was enough ink for the job. Then it checked the calendar and saw he had a meeting in ten minutes. The printer finished the pages, and Vik put them in his bag.

Mrs. Dobbs owned a small shop, and the cash machine was very noisy. She said to her phone, "What time is it in London right now? My supplier there said he would send the receipt by evening, and I want to know if he has gone home." The phone understood that she wanted the time in London. It said it was nine at night there. Mrs. Dobbs said, "Then I'll wait until tomorrow." She asked the phone to draw her attention to the message when it came, and it set an alert for ten in the morning. She counted twenty-five boxes on the shelf and went home.

Pets need food, water and walks every day. Many people use a bowl that holds water for hours, or a feeder that opens at a certain time. A pet door lets a cat or dog go in and out. Some homes have cameras that connect to the internet, so owners can see their dogs while they are away. When a new puppy arrives, people welcome it with a soft bed and a toy. People change the time of meals or the length of walks as pets grow. They say, "Feed the cat at six," "Remind me to walk Max," or "Fill the water bowl." A snowy day may mean a shorter walk.

Mina was a child on a camping trip, and her tent was far from the lake. She asked her dad's tablet, "Can you help me? Is it going to be colder tonight than last night? I want to bring double the blankets." The tablet understood that Mina wanted to know about the weather in the hills. It said that tonight would be about five degrees colder than last night. It told her to bring one more blanket and a warm hat. Mina laughed. She packed the blankets, a game and a juicy orange to share with her dad. Then she sat by the fire and watched the stars.

When you travel, prices may be in money you don't know. A coffee costs three euros in one country, but what does that mean at home? The answer depends on the exchange rate, which is the number that tells you how much one kind of money is worth in another. The rate changes from moment to moment, so people check it before they buy something. A raw number on a sign does not tell you much. People ask, "How much is that in dollars?", "What is the rate today?", or "Is it cheaper if I swim in the hotel pool than visit the beach club?" Mostly they want a price they can understand.

The speaker understood that Greg was asking for something to listen to, even though he did not say it. It asked if he wanted the audiobook his brother liked. Greg said yes, and the speaker started the book where he had stopped last time. Greg leaned back and listened.

It should go with my friends." The phone understood that Lena wanted a new contact for Mrs. Park. It asked for the phone number. Lena read it out loud. The phone saved it in the friends group and not in the work group, as she asked. Lena also said, "Don't double my old contacts, I have too many." The phone checked the list and saw no copy. A small child ran across the grass, and Lena put the phone away.

Learning another language is a bit like learning to swim. At first the words feel strange, but with practice they last. People use a phone to look up a word, hear how it sounds, or check how to spell it. They might keep a list of useful phrases for a trip. If a word feels stuck in a cage in their head, they ask again. They change the language, or the word, as they go. People say, "How do you say hello in German?", "Spell necessary for me," or "What does gracias mean?" The last question is often the best: "Can you say it slowly?"

Raj, a cook, was driving to the market before dawn with a truck full of empty cans. The radio was noisy, so he spoke up. "Hey assistant, how long will it take to get to Fulton Market if I leave tomorrow at five?" The assistant understood that he wanted the drive time to Fulton Market for a five o'clock start the next morning. It checked the roads and said the drive would take about twenty-five minutes, because there was very little traffic that early. Raj also asked it to convert the distance into miles, since the sign he remembered was in kilometers. The assistant said the market was about nine miles away. Raj thanked it, asked it to wake him at four thirty, and went back to loading the cans into the truck.

The assistant understood that she needed a hotel in Lisbon, three nights, two guests, and a quiet room that did not face the street. It found a small hotel with a pool and a room at the back, and it booked the room for her. Then it told her that check-in starts at three o'clock. Marta smiled and went back to her spreadsheet.

When you order food to your home, the app shows a price, a delivery time and a place to leave a tip. People often change a few things before they order. They change the address, the tip, or the time. Many say, "Leave it at the door" or "Bring it up to the third floor." A label on the bag tells the driver which order is yours. If the food is late, people feel sad, so the app shows where the driver is on a map. To change the tip, people say, "Make the tip bigger" or "Tip two dollars." To change the time, they say, "Bring it later" or "Deliver it at six."

Tyre pressure is how much air is inside each tyre. Too little air wears out the tyres and wastes fuel, so it is a serious thing to check. For a new driver it can feel like a puzzle, but it is simple. A gauge shows a number, and a sticker inside the car door shows the right number. If the tyre is low, people ask their assistant or the pump to put more air in. They say, "A little more air in the front tyres," or "Let some air out, it's too hard." After a long trip, a careful driver might celebrate by checking all four tyres once more.

Leo, an office worker, had a video appointment with his doctor at four. He was walking down the street to the office when he spoke to his phone. "When the doctor joins, unmute me, but don't turn my camera on. I'm outside and I don't want her to see the traffic." The assistant understood that he wanted his microphone on and his camera off. At four o'clock it joined the call, unmuted his microphone, and kept the camera off. The call was smooth. Leo explained his headache, the doctor asked a few questions, and the assistant put a reminder on his calendar for a check-up next month.

When you stay at a hotel, you book a room for a number of nights and tell them how many guests are coming. Check-in is usually in the afternoon, and check-out is in the morning. People often change the dates, the number of guests, or the kind of room. They say, "One more night," "Make it for three people," or "Can I have a room on a higher floor?" Most rooms have a kettle to boil water for tea, and if you are hungry late at night, you can ask the front desk about a snack. Staying an extra hour after check-out is also something people ask for.

Nadia had just moved to the city, and it was a cool day in autumn. In her small kitchen she opened the fridge, which was almost empty, and said, "Shopping list." The assistant understood that she wanted to see her shopping list, and it read out the items: bread, eggs and rice. Nadia wanted to enjoy a proper breakfast, so she said, "Gold apples." The assistant understood that she wanted gold apples added to the list, and it put them at the bottom. Then it asked if she would like to find the nearest store. Nadia said yes, and the assistant gave her a short walking route to a market two streets away.

The power went out in Hana's shop just before closing. She owned the little bakery on the corner, and customers were still inside. "Assistant, how long will this power cut last? Is it going to be more than an hour?" The assistant understood that she wanted to know the length of the outage. It checked the power company's page and said that the power should be back in about two hours, which was longer than she hoped. Hana wrote a note with a pencil and taped it to the door. She asked the assistant to text her two workers that they could go home early. She felt proud of how calmly everyone helped carry the bread to the back.

A meal plan is a list of what you will eat during the week. It helps you shop once, waste less food, and avoid the question of what to cook every night. People sort their meals by day, so Monday might be pasta and Tuesday might be soup. When someone is sick, or a friend comes over, they change the plan. They say, "Move the soup to Thursday," "Something light for tonight," or "No meat on Friday." For packed lunches, they ask for easy things, like "Sandwiches for the kids, three days." A good plan is simple and easy to change.

Tom was in a hurry. He was pushing a cart through the outdoor store, zooming past the tents, when he spoke to his phone. "What's the weather on the trail on Saturday? No wait, Sunday. We're leaving Sunday." The assistant understood that Tom had changed his mind and wanted the Sunday forecast. It looked at the most recent forecast for the hills and said it would be cloudy with a light rain after noon. Tom asked for a packing list for a day hike in the rain. The assistant made one: a jacket, water, a map, snacks and dry socks. Tom put a rain jacket in the cart and hurried to the checkout.

A few minutes later she asked, "Time left?" The assistant said the chapter had twenty minutes to go, and the length of the whole book was about four hours. Ana smiled and said, "Bookmark here." The assistant saved the spot.

A contact is a small card in your phone with a person's name, phone number, address and birthday. It lets you call or write to someone without remembering the number. Contacts lie in a list, in alphabetical order, so they are easy to find. People change them when someone moves or gets a new number. They say, "Change Dan's number to this one," or "Add a birthday for Aunt Rosa." Some cards have a home number and a back office number. Before saving a number on a card, many people first write it on a note stuck to the microwave.

Air in a home can get dry, dusty or stale. A purifier cleans the air by pulling it through a filter, and a humidifier adds a little water to dry air. Opening a window brings in fresh air. Bad air can be a serious problem for people with allergies. People change the speed, the room, and the time. They say, "Turn the purifier up," "Run it on low tonight," or "Make the air less dry." Most machines have a light that changes color when the air is dirty. It is good to read the note on the filter and change it when it gets gray.

Booking a table is a way to make sure there is a seat for you when you arrive. You tell the restaurant the day, the time and how many people are coming. Plans often change, so people ask to move the time, add a guest or cancel. They say things like push our table to eight, make it five people instead of four, or please cancel Friday's booking. A gentle tip: check the opening hours before you go, because some places close early. If it snows hard, a restaurant may close for the night. And if the price worries you, you can ask for the cheaper set menu or order takeaway instead.

They want to know the way to a place they need to reach.
Directions to the airport
how do i get to the station
I am sorry to bother you, but which way is Maple Street from here?
Take me to the mall, but not on the highway.
I do not want toll roads. What is the fastest way to the lake?
If the road has a problem, show me another route to my brother's house.
The ice on the road should melt by noon, so please find the clearest way to the hospital.
Could you kindly tell me how to walk to the museum from the bus stop?

Omar is a driver, and his morning was not going well. He had a flat tire, so he pulled over at a gas station to fill the tank while he waited for the repair truck. His phone buzzed with a note about a parcel from his sister. He asked, "Hey phone, has my parcel come yet?" The assistant checked his mail account and said the parcel was at the post office. Omar said, "Please ask them to keep it until tomorrow at seven, because I cannot get there today." The assistant sent a message to the post office and told him the parcel would be held until tomorrow at seven. Omar unplugged his phone charger from the dashboard and smiled. One problem, at least, was fixed.

Grandma Rosa stood in her kitchen with a cup of tea. Her tablet screen was frozen, so she pressed the button to reset it. When the screen was clear again, she said, "Please plan my dinners for this week with no fish, and put eggs on my shopping list." The tablet thought for a moment. Then it said it had planned five dinners: soup, pasta, chicken with rice, an omelette and a vegetable pie. It had also put a dozen eggs on the shopping list. Rosa asked it to read the dinners back to her. It did, one by one, and she nodded at each. "That is plenty of food for me and the cat," she said, and the tablet saved the plan.

Many medicines come with a plan. A doctor says how much to take and when, for example one pill after breakfast and one before bed. A reminder helps, because it is easy to forget. People change these reminders often. They say things like move my evening pill to nine, remind me to drink water with it, or stop the reminders after the final dose on Friday. Some people put a gold star on the calendar for every day they took their medicine. If the doctor changes the dose, you ask to update the amount instead of making a new reminder. Doctor visits work the same way: you ask to move one to next week or to a different time of day.

They want to know how many days are left until a date.
How many days until Christmas?
days till my birthday on may 9
how many dasy until the match
I will cheer for my son at the race on the 20th. How many days are left?
My brain is not sharp today. Can you count the days from now to the first of March?
I am fixing a wheel on my bike for the ride on Saturday week. How long do I have?
Could you please tell me how many days remain before our holiday starts on August 4?
How long until the weekend?

They want to start recording a video.
Record this.
start filming
start recordnig now
Hit record, my family is about to laugh at the dog.
Is the camera working? If so, please film a short clip of the kids.
Could you film the next five minutes? I want to remember this.
I would like to make a video of the garden, so please open the camera and press record.
Film my talk. The radio will be off, so it should be quiet.

Mr. Alvarez was a retired teacher who liked quiet evenings. One night a huge storm covered the street in ice, and the power went out. He felt around for his phone and said, "My lights are out. Is it only my house, or is it much bigger?" The assistant looked at the power company's page and said about half of the town had no power, and that the repairs would continue through the night. Mr. Alvarez asked, "Please report the cut on Oak Street, and turn on my flashlight." The assistant sent the report and switched on the flashlight. It also said the repair might take twice as long as usual because of the ice. Mr. Alvarez found a candle and a blanket and waited.

Person: Read me the news, but keep it shorter than yesterday.
Assistant: Sure. Which kind of news do you want: local, sports or world?
Person: Local. I would like to hear about the garden show.
Assistant: The garden show is in September, and the paper says there will be a neat display of roses. Do you want two more stories?
Person: Yes, two more. I have to speak at my club tonight and I want something to talk about.
Assistant: Okay. The first is about a new bus stop on Mill Road. The second is about a school choir that won a prize.

Lena was a student with a big test the next day and an empty stomach. She had ordered food online an hour ago, and nothing had come. She looked at her phone and said, "I have been starving for an hour, and my doorbell is silent." The assistant understood that she was asking about her order. It opened the shop's page and said the driver was ten minutes away. Then Lena saw the app showed her old street. "That is wrong," she said. "Please fix my address." The assistant changed the address to her new flat and sent the driver a message. Ten minutes later, her food arrived, still hot.

Person: I need to put something in the thing for my granddaughter's homework.
Assistant: I can help. Do you want a reminder, or a note?
Person: A reminder. The girl has to hand in her story.
Assistant: What day and time should I remind you?
Person: Tomorrow at seven in the evening.
Assistant: Do you want a daily reminder until then?
Person: No, once is enough. I stand by the kitchen door at that time every evening, so I will notice.
Assistant: Done. I will remind you tomorrow at seven.

A thermostat tells your heating when to work. You pick a temperature, and the heater turns on when the room is colder and turns off when it is warm enough. Some homes have a weak radiator in the back room, so people turn that one up. Many thermostats also record how long the heating ran each day, which helps you see what you use. People change the heating by saying things like make it a little warmer, set the bedroom to eighteen, or turn it down at night. A small tip: on a cold morning, you can warm a cup of tea in the microwave while the room heats up.

Mr. Patel owned a small sweet shop, and he was always friendly to his customers. On a slow morning he sat behind the counter with a piece of chocolate and said to his phone, "Tell me the football scores from last night and read me the top headline." The assistant understood that he wanted two things. First, it read the scores of three matches, and the home team had won. Then it read the top headline, which was about a new bridge in the city. Mr. Patel asked it to wait while a customer paid for a bar of chocolate. The assistant stopped reading. When he came back, he said, "Go on," and it finished the story.

Gus was a gardener with sore eyes at the end of a long day. His hands were dry from the soil, and he did not want to touch the screen. He held up a pill bottle and said, "Make the text on this phone bigger and read my messages out loud." The assistant understood both things. It made the letters on the screen twice as large and began to read. The first message was from a customer who wanted a new design for a flower bed. The second was from his sister, who asked if he was coming to dinner. Gus said, "Tell her yes," and the assistant sent the answer.

Mei had just moved to the city, and her new building had a small pool on the roof. She did not know how it worked. She stood by the water and said, "Is this pool warm enough to swim, and how do I turn on the pump?" The assistant understood she wanted two things. It looked at the building's pool page and told her the water was twenty-four degrees. Then it turned on the pump with the building's control panel and said the cleaning would take an hour. Mei asked it to print the pool rules for her. The page was full of small rules, but she read them all. Behind her, a mountain of clouds slowly moved over the city.

name: wake_me_up
does: Sets an alarm for a time or a number of minutes, and wakes you gently.
inputs: the time or how long to sleep, and how loud the alarm should be
people say:
- Get me up at six tomorrow.
- Wake me in twenty minutes, I am just having a nap.
- My old clock is broken, so please be my alarm.
- The ship leaves at nine, so I must be up early.
- I need to be in the corn field before sunrise.
- Don't let me sleep past noon.

name: laundry_timer
does: Tells you when a wash or dry cycle is finished and keeps a file of your past cycles.
inputs: which machine, and how many minutes are left
people say:
- Tell me when my clothes are ready.
- I am going out to plant tomatoes, so shout when the dryer is done.
- How long is left on the wash?
- Is the machine finished yet?
- Let me know when the towels stop spinning.
- What did I wash last Tuesday?

They want to change a recipe to feed a different number of people.
Double it.
Make it for six.
Half the recipe, please.
I am cooking for four, not two. Can you change the amounts?
Please write the red sauce again for ten people.
I need to dress the salad for twelve, so scale that part up.
There are only three of us tonight. Can you shrink everything to fit?
Could you kindly turn this cake recipe into one for a big family of eight?

They want to put something on the shopping list.
Put milk on my list.
need eggs
put bread on the lst
We are out of rice. Please note it down for the next shop.
I teach a class tonight and need to mix juice for the kids, so write down orange juice.
For the main dish I need chicken, so put that on the list too.
The fridge is empty of butter. Can you remind me to buy some?
Could you please add cheese to what I need from the store?

A baby monitor lets you hear and see your baby from another room. It has a small microphone near the baby's bed, and it sends the sound to a speaker or phone. When the baby makes a noise, you can hear it right away. Most parents change a few things. They say turn the sound up, make the screen dim at night, or tell me if the baby cries. Some monitors have a silver light on the front that shows when they are on. Feeding and nap times work with reminders. A parent might say remind me to feed the baby at three, or wake me when the nap is over, even if they fly home late and miss the clock.

name: set_drink_style
does: Changes how strong, sweet or creamy a hot drink is made.
inputs: the drink, how strong, how sweet, and how much milk
people say:
- Make my coffee creamy today.
- Less sugar, please, my tea is too sweet.
- I will be at the mailbox, so have my latte ready in five minutes.
- Fold in a bit more milk.
- I want it strong, like yesterday.
- Not so bitter this time.

Priya had just woken up when she heard a drip in the bathroom. She sat up in bed and said to her phone, "Excuse me, could you please check if water is running anywhere in the house? I heard a strange drip in the night and I am worried about the pipes." The assistant understood she wanted a leak check. It looked at the water meter, which was still moving even though no tap was open. The assistant told her this might mean a leak, maybe in the pipe that connects the sink to the wall. It offered to shut off the main water valve, and Priya said yes. The assistant closed it and said the chicken in the sink would have to wait for fresh water. Priya laughed and called a plumber.

A football match is the main event of the week for many fans. Each match has a score, a start time and two teams. People use a phone or speaker to follow them. They ask for changes like send me the new score, tell me when the match starts, or follow my team this season. Training works in a similar way. A runner might say how far did I go today, or hang up a plan to run a longer distance each week. The distance of a run is often shown in kilometres. When a team plays away, fans also ask how long the trip will take, so they can plan the day.

A washing machine cleans clothes with water, soap and a spinning drum. You choose a cycle, a heat and a size of load. Small loads need less water, and big loads need more. People change these things by saying wash on cold, use a short cycle, or spin it again. A dryer works in the same way, with heat instead of water. If a stain is left on a shirt after washing, you can try again before you dry it, because heat can make it stay. To get a stain out, many people rub it with soap first. Folding comes last. You can fold the left sleeve over the right one, then fold the shirt in half.

name: send_party_invites
does: Sends an invitation to your guests with the date, the time and the place.
inputs: the guest names, the date and time, and the place
people say:
- Tell everyone about my party on Saturday.
- Ask the neighbours to come for breakfast on Sunday.
- My cousins have to travel far, so let them know early.
- Warn my guests to bring heavy coats, it will be cold.
- Tell Anna and Ben to come at six.

Jake was late for work, and his shoes were still in his hand. The phone in his pocket would not stop ringing, and the constant noise made him nervous. He said, "Excuse me, could you please pay my electricity bill today? I got a message that it is due tomorrow, and I will be on a plane all day." The assistant understood he wanted the bill paid before the due date. It opened the bank page and found the bill for forty-two dollars. It paid it and said the payment was done. Then Jake asked it to reset the phone's ringer to quiet. The assistant did that too, and the noise stopped. Jake ran out the door.

A bike ride is easy to plan with a phone. You choose a start and an end, and the phone shows the route and the distance. It can also tell you the speed you are going and how long you have been riding. People often change a ride. They say take me on a flatter route, make it a shorter ride, or compare this ride with last week. A light bike weighs only a few pounds more than a bag of apples, so hills are not so hard. It is great to check the weather too. Many riders ask will it rain at four, then change the plan if it will.

Bill was a driver, and he needed a few papers before he left for work. His oven timer was beeping in the kitchen, and it was snowing outside. He said, "Print two copies of my delivery list, and use less ink than last time." The assistant understood he wanted two pages and a lighter print. It sent the list to the printer and chose the draft setting, which saves ink. Then it told him the ink was half full, and there were only a few sheets of paper left. Bill put more paper in the tray. The pages came out in a minute, and he put them in his bag.

name: forward_my_mail
does: Sends your letters to your new address after you move house.
inputs: the old address, the new address, and the date to start
people say:
- I am moving next week, send my letters to my new place.
- Keep my post from going to the old flat.
- Hold my letters at the post office until I am settled, I will be late to pick them up.
- Tell the post office I live on Pine Road now.
- My lemon tree stays but I am off to Leeds, so send the bills there.

Gus, the gardener, stood in the sunny kitchen and looked at his curtains. He had paid a lot for them, but they were fading. He said to the speaker, "Close the blinds on the south window, but don't close the whole room. I do not want to sit in the dark." The assistant understood he wanted only one window shaded. It closed the blinds on the south window and left the others open. Then Gus said, "And please do not forget to open them again at five. These curtains are too expensive to ruin, and that person from the shop told me to keep them out of the sun." The assistant set a reminder and opened them again at five.

name: remember_birthday
does: Saves a person's birthday in your account and reminds you before the day.
inputs: the person's name, the date, and how many days before to remind you
people say:
- Note that Dad's birthday is on March 3.
- Don't let me forget Anna's day next month.
- My calendar is full, so tell me a week early about Tom's party.
- Remind me about Grandma's birthday and what she likes.
- Which birthdays are coming up?

They want to see how many people liked their post.
How many likes did I get?
Did my beach photo get more likes than the last one?
I do not care about the comments, just tell me the likes.
I am too tired to scroll. Can you just tell me if more people saw today's post than yesterday's?
Has anyone liked my picture yet?
What is the number of likes on my last post, and is it half of what I had last week?
Could you please check my page and tell me if my new post is doing better than the old one?

Arithmetic is the part of math we use every day. We learn it in the very first lesson at school. We add numbers to see how much we have, take them away to see what is left, multiply to find the total of equal groups, and divide to share things. People use it when they shop, cook or split a bill. They ask for it in many ways. Some say what is twelve and eight, others say take five off thirty, or share a hundred between four. If you make a mistake, you can say start again or restart from zero. A big sum may be hard to do in your head, so many people simply ask a phone. It gives the answer in a second.

Person: water the plnats out front
Assistant: Which ones do you mean, the pots by the door or the flower beds?
Person: The pots. They look dry. And the pretty ones in the window box too.
Assistant: How long should I run the water?
Person: Ten minutes. It is June and the sun is strong, and I did not sleep well, so I forgot yesterday.
Assistant: Okay. I will start the sprinkler for the pots and the window box for ten minutes.

Mr. Hale held his phone as if it were a hot plate. He had dreamed of a clean white jacket from a shop in Canada, but he did not know the price in his money. He looked at the grey sky and said, "How much is a hundred dollars in pounds? No, wait, I mean a hundred and fifty." The assistant understood the correction. It looked up the exchange rate for that day and said a hundred and fifty Canadian dollars was about ninety-one pounds. Mr. Hale said, "That is not so bad," and asked it to save the number in his notes. The assistant saved it. He smiled and put the phone down gently.

They want to be reminded to do something at a certain time.
Remind me at five.
Remind me to take my coat and call mum at five.
Tell me to restart the router tonight.
Please nudge me often, every hour, to stand up and stretch.
I always forget my keys, so say something when I leave.
Could you ping me on Friday morning to pay the rent and book the dentist?
Don't let me forget the bins before I go to bed.

Sam was a cook in a busy restaurant, and the kitchen had a constant noise of pans and fans. A video meeting was about to start, and he had lost the password for the call. He wiped his hands and said, "Join call." The assistant understood he wanted to join the meeting on his tablet. It opened the meeting and filled in the saved password. Sam could see his boss and three others, and they asked him to follow the list of the new menu on the screen. He said, "Share screen," and the assistant shared his menu with the group. The boss smiled, and Sam went back to the stove.

Old Henry was a gardener, and he had a laptop with a wireless mouse that he rarely used. That morning he was looking at a photo of the old bridge in town, when a message warned him that the battery was low. The screen blinked. He frowned and said, "Restart laptop." The assistant understood he wanted the computer to start again. It saved his photo, closed the open pages and restarted the laptop. A minute later the screen came back. Henry said, "Plug in." The assistant told him to connect the charger and said it would tell him when the battery was full. Henry found the cable under a pile of seed bags.

Mrs. Green was a retired teacher who was flying to see her son the next morning. Before bed she sat in her chair and said to the speaker, "Excuse me, could you please arm the house alarm and turn on the camera at the front door? I am leaving early and I want to be sure the house is safe while I am gone." The assistant armed the alarm and switched on the camera. Then it told her the left window in the kitchen was open. Mrs. Green thanked it and went to close the window. She came back, and the assistant checked once more. All the doors were locked, and she poured a glass of wine and went to bed.

Mr. Brown did not like technology, but he liked his ideas. One afternoon he sat on a hill behind his house, and a fine idea for a poem came to him. He held up his phone and said, "Excuse me, could you please write this down for me? I am afraid I will forget it before I get home, and my pencil has a loose end and keeps breaking." The assistant understood he wanted a note. It opened the notes page and wrote the words he said, one line at a time. When he stopped, the assistant read the poem back to him. Mr. Brown nodded, and the note was saved for later.

Tara was a student, and she had to go to the train station at six. It was raining and a bitter wind was blowing. She did not want to wait outside, so she said to her phone, "Book me a ride, but not a shared one, and please do not send a car that is far away." The assistant understood she wanted a private ride with a close car. It booked a car with a driver two minutes away and told her the pickup spot was the door of her building. Tara put her napkin and her bag in her coat and waited inside. The car arrived in two minutes.

They want to know how much money in one currency is worth in another.
How many euros is a hundred dollars?
I wonder if my dollars will go far in Japan.
I wish I knew if my pounds will buy me a lot in Spain.
I sold my old lawn mower, and I would like to spend the money in Mexico. Is that a good idea?
I am going away in the mild days of spring. Is it cheap to eat out there?
My sister sent me twenty euros. What is that in my money?
Could you tell me if the money is worth more or less than last month?

They want to write a text message to a friend.
Text Sam that I am late.
Tell mum I am home, but don't send it to the group.
Message Ana to bring the magazine. Keep it short.
Say hi to Joe. Tell him I am at the new flat and still need to unpack.
Write to Lily that I am comfortable on the couch and will not come out tonight.
Could you send my brother a text and say that I do not want to go to the party?
Reply to the last message, but do not use any long words.

Mr. Wood did not like phones. One morning the water from his kitchen tap came out brown, and he was not sure what to do. He had a lesson with a neighbour in an hour, so he could not wait. He picked up the speaker and said, "Book repair." The assistant did not know which repair he meant, but it asked, "Is it for the tap in the kitchen?" Mr. Wood said yes. The assistant found a plumber who was free in the afternoon and booked a visit for two o'clock. It sent him a message with the time. Mr. Wood did not want a lot of fuss, and he was glad that was all there was to it.

Nora was a nurse, and she came home at seven in the morning after a night shift. The house was quiet, and she was so tired that she could hardly feel her feet. She dropped her bag, opened the fridge and found only half a sandwich. She said to the speaker, "We are out of food. Please put bread, eggs and soup on my list, and have it delivered tomorrow at seven." The assistant put the three things on the list. Then it asked the shop to send the groceries tomorrow at seven in the morning. It told Nora the order was set. She ate the half sandwich and went to sleep.

Dana was an office worker, and she ate a slice of melon at her desk while she swept the crumbs into her hand. Her office was in a tall building, and she had to leave early for the airport. She said to her phone, "When does the Denver flight leave, and is it on time?" The assistant understood she wanted two answers. It looked at the airline's departure page. It told her the flight left at 4:40 and was twenty minutes late. It added that the gate was B12. Dana thanked it and packed her bag. She had time for one more slice of melon.

Person: Can you open the blinds and unlock the front door?
Assistant: I can open the blinds. Which room should I do first?
Person: The first floor. I paid a big sum for this flat and I still do not know how the blinds work.
Assistant: Okay, I opened the blinds on the first floor. I am sorry, but I cannot unlock doors. That is not something I can do.
Person: That is fine. I will use the key.
Assistant: Do you want me to open the blinds upstairs too?
Person: Yes, please.

Shopping from home is easy. You pick something, choose a size, and the shop sends it to your door. People use a phone or a speaker to do it. They change their orders by saying things like send it to my work address, make it a larger size, or cancel the second one. If an item does not fit, you ask to return it, and the shop sends a label. A lovely thing about delivery is that you can see where your package is. Some people say tell me when it is at the door, or keep the parcel cool, if it has food that must stay fresh. At night they sometimes look at the moon and wait.

A printer puts words and pictures from your phone or computer onto paper. It needs ink and paper to work. When the ink is low, a yellow light may come on. People ask for small changes, like print two copies, print only the first page, or make it black and white to save ink. A scanner does the opposite. It takes a paper and turns it into a file on your screen. You can scroll through a long scan to check that every page is there. People say scan this letter, save it as a picture, or send it to my email. Some printers do both jobs, and most have a pencil-thin button to start.

Ravi was late for the bus, with a napkin still stuck in his hand from breakfast. His thumb was sore from typing all morning, so he talked to his phone instead.

'Mute notifications,' he said.

The phone understood that he wanted the alerts from his social media app to go quiet. It turned them off and said they would stay off until he asked for them again. Ravi nodded and jogged toward the stop.

Then he remembered his cousin's photo from last night. 'Like it,' he said. The phone found the newest post from his cousin and tapped the like button. A small heart showed up under the picture.

'Now stop the video,' he added, because a clip was still playing on the screen. The phone paused it. Ravi smiled, put the napkin in his pocket, and got on the bus just in time.

Mrs. Alvarez sat at her desk with a pencil and a crossword. It was past seven, and her stomach had been growling for an hour.

'My fridge is empty and my feet are tired,' she said to her tablet.

She never said the word dinner, but the assistant understood. It opened her food delivery app and showed her the last thing she had ordered, a bowl of noodle soup from a place on Maple Street. 'Same again?' it asked.

'Yes, please. That was easy last time,' she said.

The assistant placed the order. It explained that the restaurant did not ship far, so a rider from nearby would bring the soup in about twenty minutes. Mrs. Alvarez went back to her crossword. When the bell rang, the soup was still hot.

Jo was texting her friend Priya when she remembered the tomato plants. They had looked dry all week. She picked up her phone and typed, 'the tomatoes look sad. they need more water.'

The assistant understood that Jo wanted the back garden sprinklers to run for longer. It did not ask any more questions. It changed the sprinkler plan from ten minutes to twenty-five minutes and told her the new time would start tomorrow morning.

Jo wrote back, 'ok thx.' Then she remembered the garden party on Saturday and asked what the weather would be like. The assistant said the day would be dry and sunny, so she could dress lightly. Jo sent Priya a thumbs up and went back to their chat.

A bike route is a path from one place to another that suits people on bicycles. It is for staying on quiet streets and cycle paths instead of busy roads. People often change a route to fit their day. They might say make it shorter, avoid the steep hills, or find me something flat. A club might invite friends for a Sunday ride and share a recent route that ends at a cafe with warm pancakes. Riders also ask about their ride afterwards. How far did I go? How fast was I on the last hill? How long did it take? A good route is easy to follow and fits the time you have.

They want the assistant to wake them with an alarm.
wake me at seven
alarm for tomorrow at seven please
I have an early train, so can you get me up tomorrow at seven
set my automatic wake-up for tomorrow at seven
ring me out of bed at seven, and make it a slow, gentle sound like waves on sand
can you describe the alarm sounds you have and pick the softest one for tomorrow at seven
make sure I do not sleep in tomorrow, I have to be out of the house by eight
buzz me at 7 tomorrow

Dana was packing lunches while the kids ran around looking for their shoes. The bus was due in five minutes. As always, she felt a small worry about the house.

'I never know if the garage is shut when we fly out of here in the morning,' she said to the speaker on the shelf.

The assistant took this as a question about the garage door. It checked the door sensor and said the door was still open. 'Do you want me to close it?' it asked.

'Yes, please,' said Dana.

The door came down. The assistant told her it was closed and that the front door was locked too. It was so easy that Dana laughed. She grabbed the lunches, counted three kids, and hurried out into the cold.

Most people use a phone or a screen to find a film. You can look for what is on tonight, watch a trailer, or check the cinema times near your home. People change a few things when they ask. They might say show me something funny, find a film that is not scary, or what is on after dinner. Some people hate loud action films, and others only want a spicy thriller. Families often ask for something short, so the little ones can stay awake. A cinema may also tell you how long a film is. A long one can run almost three hours, which feels like carrying a kilogram of popcorn on your lap.

Grandpa Leo sat in the basement next to the old dehumidifier. It had an automatic switch that turned it on and off, and he did not care for the noise it made. Upstairs, his grandsons were coming for supper.

'Get us two large pizzas, plain cheese, from the place on Elm Street,' he told his phone.

The assistant opened the food delivery app and found the shop. It put two large cheese pizzas in the basket and asked, 'Would you like to leave a tip for the driver?'

'Twenty percent, please. They drive in all kinds of weather,' said Leo.

The assistant added the tip and told him the pizzas would arrive in about thirty minutes. Leo turned off the basement light and went up to set the table.

Grandma Rosa was excited. Her granddaughter had a school concert tonight, and she wanted to study the parking situation before she left the house.

'Find me a parking spot near the school hall for seven o'clock,' she told her phone.

The assistant searched and showed two car parks close to the hall. One was free and one cost three dollars an hour.

Then Rosa remembered how crowded it always got. 'No, wait. Make that six thirty. I want to be early and find a good seat.'

The assistant understood she meant the arrival time, not the concert time. It changed the plan to six thirty, picked the free car park, and said it would remind her to leave at six. Rosa picked up her coat and her camera and smiled.

Maya got home after a long night shift. Her eyes were heavy, and she wanted to lie down, but she knew she would forget something important.

'Remind me to take my pants to the cleaner when I walk past the square this afternoon,' she said to her phone. 'Don't remind me tonight, and please don't make it loud. I'll be asleep.'

The assistant understood that the reminder should happen at a place, not at a time. It set a reminder for when she was near the town square later that day. It also said it would not send anything tonight, and it turned off the sound for this reminder so it would only show a small message.

Maya thanked it, pulled the curtains shut, and fell asleep within a minute.

Food delivery lets you order a meal from a restaurant and have it brought to your door. You pick the dishes, check the address, and see how long it will take. People change things a lot. They ask for less spice, an extra side, or a later time. Many people owe a small thank you to the driver, so they add a tip. My uncle is careful with his orders. He says he wants it hot, not too salty, and at the door by seven. If the food is late, you can ask where the driver is. If you made a mistake, you can say cancel that order or change the address.

We measure things so that other people know how big, heavy or hot something is. Sometimes people use different units, like meters and feet, or kilograms and pounds. Say you are on a video call and tell your sister that the bathroom is two meters wide. She only knows feet, so she asks, how much is that? You unmute and say it is about six and a half feet. People ask for these changes with words like how many feet is that, what is it in pounds, or give me that in Celsius. Even a shallow pool has to be measured. The shallow end might be four feet deep, which is a little more than a meter.

A kitchen has many machines that help us cook. An oven heats food, a kettle boils water, and a coffee machine makes a hot drink. A dishwasher cleans plates while you rest. On a sunny morning, many people turn on the kettle first. They change the temperature, the time, or the program. They say things like bake it for ten more minutes, make the water hotter, or run the short wash. My dog likes to sit by the oven when something smells good. A heavy cast iron pan works on the stove and in the oven, so you can start it on the fire and finish it in the heat. Always wait for hot things to cool.

A podcast is a show you can listen to whenever you like. An audiobook is a book read aloud, often in chapters. Both remember where you stopped, so you do not have to wait or search when you come back. People use them on walks, on trains, and while they cook. They change a few things. They speed up a slow voice, jump to the next chapter, or go back thirty seconds to hear a sentence again. They say play faster, skip ahead, or where did I leave off? Your goal is to enjoy the story without trouble. If the end of a chapter is close, you can ask for one more episode before bed.

Tomas was a gardener, and on his lunch break he was writing a short note for the garden club. He sat on a bench with one tired foot on a bucket and spoke to his phone.

'How many words do I have so far?' he asked.

The assistant counted and said there were ninety-eight words. Tomas wanted the note to be short, so he said, 'Tell me if it goes over one hundred and twenty.' The assistant said it would.

He read the note on the screen. The letters were small, so he said, 'Raise the text size.' The assistant made the letters bigger. Tomas fixed one spelling mistake in the word tomatoes, and wrote about how healthy the roses looked this spring. Then he finished his sandwich.

Grandpa Ned could not sleep. The alarm clock beside his bed was so loud that he kept waking up half asleep, just waiting for it. He wanted a change, but he did not know how to explain it.

'The alarm is too loud,' he said to the speaker on the table. 'Make it half as loud, and start it softer.'

The assistant understood that he meant the morning alarm. It cut the volume to half and set the sound to rise slowly instead of starting at full strength. It also asked if he wanted the old alarm to stay, and Ned said no.

Before bed, the old clock was hidden in a drawer. Ned rolled over, closed his eyes, and slept all the way until the soft chime came.

Person: Twelve Birch Lane. I want to get to the clinic twenty minutes before my visit.
Assistant: Thank you. What time is your visit?
Person: Ten o'clock.
Assistant: Then I will book a taxi for nine fifteen. The minimum fare is eight dollars. Shall I add a note for the driver?
Person: Yes, please say I walk slowly.

Priya came home after her night shift with her eyes half closed. In two days, her family would celebrate the winter holiday, and the house still had no lights. She dropped her bag on the sofa and spoke to the speaker.

'Play carols,' she said.

The assistant started a playlist of holiday songs at a low volume. Priya smiled. 'Lights on,' she said next. The assistant switched on the string of lights around the window. 'Timer ten,' she added. It set a timer for ten minutes, and Priya put a pan of potatoes on to fry, with the minimum of fuss. Her family and her whole network of cousins would be coming, and she wanted the first batch to be ready. When the timer rang, she was almost asleep, with the lights glowing behind her.
