Every home uses electricity, and the amount changes with the day. Lights, the fridge, the heating and a laptop for homework all use some. Solar panels catch the sun, even on a pale winter day, and turn it into power for the house. People change their habits to save energy. They turn off lights, lower the heating, or run the washing machine at night when power is cheaper. They say things like how much power did I use today, switch off the lights downstairs, or cancel the heating for tonight. A small change each day can lower the bill. It also helps to know which machines use the most.

A radio brings voices and music from far away. You tune it to a station, and a calm voice reads the news, plays a song, or tells you the weather. Years ago, a waiter in a small cafe might turn the radio on for his customers. Today, many people ask a speaker to do it. They say put on the radio, find a news station, or turn it down a little. Some people whisper at night, so the sound must be low. Others want a different station for each part of the day. They say change the station, play something else, or what is this song? The radio is a simple way to hear what is happening.

Hana's laptop battery was at ten percent, and her meeting started in two minutes. Her baby was crying in the next room. She was a busy parent, and she had no time to waste.

'Join my work call,' she told her phone. The assistant opened the calendar, found the meeting and joined it. The video was bright, but the screen was a plain white page.

'Share my notes, but only half of the screen,' Hana said. 'And turn the volume down by half, the baby is loud.'

The assistant understood both parts. It set the call to share one half of her screen and lowered the volume. Then it reminded her to plug in the laptop. Hana set the charger on the floor beside her chair and joined the talk with a smile.

Hector was a cook, and his hands were tired from slicing onions all day. Tonight, he wanted to start a workout at home.

'Start a leg workout with three sets of ten squats,' he told his phone. A moment later he said, 'No, make it twelve, not ten.'

The assistant understood that he was fixing a number. It changed the plan to three sets of twelve and began a timer for the first set. It also asked about the rest, and Hector said sixty seconds.

Halfway through, his knee felt strange. 'That seems dangerous,' he said to the assistant. 'Should I stop?' The assistant said that a person should stop if something hurts, and it paused the workout. Hector sat down, drank some water, and tried again tomorrow.

Walter was not good with technology. He had a small speaker at home that his daughter had given him, and he rarely used it. Tonight he felt nervous. A holiday was starting tomorrow, and he had to travel early by train. The house was chilly, and the bed was cold.

Walter smiled, put his bag by the door, and went to sleep under two blankets.

Cars need small things to keep them working. They need fuel, air in the tyres, and a little care. A car alarm makes a loud noise if someone tries to open the doors. You can also set a reminder alarm for when your parking time runs out. People change many things about their cars. They ask to warm up the engine before a cold trip, check the tyre pressure, or find out where they left the car. They say things like where did I park, how much fuel is left, or start the car. Friends sometimes split the cost of fuel on a long trip. A local garage can help when something looks wrong.

Ines was a shop owner, and she was excited because tonight was her first night away on holiday. She was locking the shop at the end of the day, and the street was quiet. She had a cookie in one hand and her phone in the other.

She typed in a hurry, 'turn on the alarm at the shpo.'

The assistant knew she meant the shop. It switched on the alarm and the door sensors. It also woke the camera at the back door. It told her, 'The shop alarm is on. Your cousin will arrive tomorrow at eight to open it.' Ines had asked it to tell him the code, and it had sent him a private message.

She finished her cookie, checked the lock once more, and went home to pack.

Sam was a busy parent who only had twenty minutes for exercise. The baby was asleep, and the kitchen floor was clean enough to stand on.

'Give me a short workout, medium speed, with double the squats from yesterday,' Sam said to the speaker.

The assistant remembered that Sam had done ten squats the day before. It made a plan with twenty squats, then push-ups and a short plank, and it set the pace to medium. It counted each round out loud.

Halfway through, Sam started to sing along to the song in the background and almost lost count. 'Do half again,' Sam gasped, meaning the last set. The assistant repeated half the set, which was ten. Sam wiped a mouth full of sweat on a towel and finished.

Omar was a driver who spent most of his week in the car. This morning he was waiting for a customer, and he wanted a few things done before the next trip. He did not want to turn the heater up himself.

'Warm up the front seats, and do not send me on the highway,' he said to the car's assistant. 'The fees are too high this week.'

The assistant understood both parts. It turned on the seat heaters. It also changed the route for the next ride so it used city streets, and it told him the ride would take eleven minutes longer. 'Is that okay?' it asked.

'Fine,' said Omar. The customer got in, and the car was warm and ready.

Accessibility settings help people use a phone or computer in the way that suits them. A person with weak eyes may want bigger text. Someone who cannot see the screen may want the device to read it aloud. Others may prefer to talk instead of tap. People change the settings with simple words. They say make the letters bigger, read this page to me, or dim the screen, it hurts my eyes. If a word is wrong, they can say no, that is not right, and say it again. Voice control lets a person open an app, call a friend, or turn a page without touching the device. These tools make the same device easier for everyone.

Some people wake up with a podcast every morning, and they know the voice better than their neighbors. A podcast app keeps a list of shows and plays the newest episode. In the summer, many people listen while they walk or sit in the garden. They often change how fast the voice talks. They say play it faster, slow it down, or go back thirty seconds. If a show is long, they may listen to half now and half later. The app remembers where you stopped. You can also say play the next episode, what is this one about, or stop this at the end of the chapter. A sleep timer will turn it off when you fall asleep.

Ahmed was a gardener, and the morning was cold. His hands were stiff, but there was a lot to do before lunch. Now and then he forgot to rest, and his back hurt.

'Start timer,' he said to his phone. The assistant started a thirty minute work timer, which was the one he usually used.

He dug for a while and moved a heavy pot of flowers into the sun. When the timer rang, he said, 'Take a break.' The assistant understood and set a ten minute rest. It also made the phone go quiet, so no messages would bother him.

Ahmed sat on a stool with a cup of tea and watched a bird in the hedge. When the break was over, he said, 'Again,' and the timer started once more.

In an emergency, a few simple things can keep you safe. A smoke alarm makes a loud noise when it smells smoke, so you can leave the house quickly. If the power goes out, a flashlight helps in the dark. A silent house is not always a safe house, so test your alarm every month. In heavy rain, a leaf can block a drain and cause flooding in the street. If water rises, do not drive through it. People ask for help with words like call the fire brigade, turn off the alarm, or send my location to my sister. After a false alarm, they may say silence it. Know the number to call for help.

Kai was walking home from school with a package under one arm. A little earlier, his friends had taken a funny picture of a puppy on a skateboard. They joked that it would grow into a huge dog and never fit on the board again. Kai wanted to send the picture, but both hands were full, so he spoke to his phone.

He typed in a hurry, 'send the last pic to mom and to my frends.'

The assistant understood who he meant by mom and found the newest photo in his gallery. It showed the photo of the puppy and asked, 'Is this the one?'

'Yes,' said Kai. The assistant sent it to his mom and to the group chat called Friends. Kai felt calm. He would not have to stop in the street. Soon his phone buzzed with laughing faces.

Mr. Dunn was not good with technology, but today he had to get to the dentist, and his car was in the garage. His neighbor had shown him how to use the assistant on his phone, so he tried it.

'Book me a taxi and tell me when it arrives,' he said slowly.

The assistant understood that he had asked two things. It booked a ride to the dentist's office and said it would tell him when the car was near. 'Where should the driver meet you?' it asked.

'At the front of my house,' said Mr. Dunn. 'And remind me to lock the door.'

The assistant showed the driver's name and picture on the screen. Ten minutes later it said, 'Your taxi is here.' Mr. Dunn locked the door and went out.

Privacy is about who can see what is yours. A password keeps your things closed to strangers. A good password is long and hard to guess. A word like lemon is easy for someone to try, but lemon with other words and numbers is better. A lock on your phone keeps people out if you lose it. Many people prefer a fingerprint, but on a humid day wet fingers do not always work, so they use a code. People change passwords when they think someone might know the old one. They say change my password, lock my phone, or who can see my photos? It is a good habit to keep your secret words to yourself.

Grandma Elsie liked to start her day with a walk, but her knees did not like the cold. She stood by the window, looked at the grey sky, and asked her speaker for help.

'Is it going to rain before the school bell rings this afternoon?' she asked. 'I run to pick up the children.'

The assistant understood that she meant the afternoon pick up. It said there was a small chance of rain at three, and the temperature would stay near twenty degrees.

'What should I wear?' she asked.

The assistant suggested a light coat and a small umbrella. Elsie wanted to stay healthy, so she also took a scarf. She smiled, picked up her bag, and went out into the day.

Nora came home from the hospital, tired after a night shift, and wanted a short rest before doing something she loved. She sat in her armchair with a ball of yarn and spoke to her phone.

'Could you please schedule an hour for knitting this afternoon at four? I would like to finish the next chapter of my pattern before my friend visits on Saturday, and I think I'll feel better if I plan it.'

The assistant understood that she wanted a time block. It put knitting on her calendar for four o'clock, for one hour. It also set a gentle reminder ten minutes before.

Nora thanked it. She closed her eyes for a short nap, and when the reminder came she woke up ready to knit.

Lena had just woken up, and her head was still full of sleep. The kitchen smelled like a burned piece of toast, so she knew it was not a day for cooking. She sat by the fish tank and spoke to her phone.

'Order a bagel with cream cheese and tell me how close the driver is,' she said.

The assistant opened the food delivery app. It understood that she had asked two things. First, it ordered a bagel with cream cheese from the cafe around the corner. Then it checked the map and said the driver was only four minutes away.

Lena stretched, fed the fish, and waited by the door. When the bell rang, the bagel was warm in its paper bag.

Baking turns simple things like flour, water and heat into bread, cakes and cookies. Dough needs time to rise, and then it needs the right heat. A cake might bake for forty minutes, and a batch of cookies for ten. Every oven is a little different, so people watch the clock. They change times and heat with words like ten more minutes, a bit hotter, or take it out now. You boil water for some recipes, but not for bread. A second look through the glass door can tell you if the top is golden. A straight knife in the middle of a cake should come out clean when it is ready.

A smart speaker is a small device that listens and plays sound. It can play music, tell you the time, and answer simple questions. It may be only one foot tall, but a heavy bass can fill a room. People often put one speaker in the kitchen and another in the bedroom. They can group speakers so the same song plays in every room. They say make it louder, lower the volume, or play in the whole house. If a speaker is not needed, they ask to disconnect it from the group. Some speakers know different voices, so they can answer each person in their own way. They are easy to move from room to room.

On Wednesday afternoon, Priya burned her hand on the office kettle. "Hey phone, my hand is burned, what do I do?" she said. The assistant understood that she had a small burn and wanted first aid steps. It told her to hold the burn under cool running water for twenty minutes, to skip the ice, and not to pop any blisters. Priya walked to the sink, and the assistant set a timer for her. It also asked if the burn was bigger than her palm. She said no, so it said she could treat it at home and should see a doctor if it got worse. Later she emptied out the first aid box to find a bandage, and the assistant reminded her to use a clean, dry one. By evening her hand felt well again.

Person: Yes please. The brand name on the bill is ClearFlow.
Assistant: Okay, I opened the ClearFlow payment page for you.

Dana was peeling oranges for the kids when the baby began to cry. Her hands were sticky, so she called out, "Play something calm for the little ones, and keep it low." The assistant understood that she wanted soft music at a quiet volume. It started a lullaby playlist and turned the sound down to about a quarter. A few songs later Dana said, "Skip this one," and the assistant moved to the next song. Since she had a free minute, she asked it to make a playlist of twenty-five songs for the car ride to her mother's house. The assistant built one from the songs she played most and said it would last about an hour and a half. During the long stretch of road that afternoon, the kids hummed along from the back seat.

A contact is a small card in your phone with a name, a number, and sometimes an address or a birthday. It is there so you never have to remember every number. People change their contacts all the time. A friend moves, so you say, "Change Sam's address." A new teacher calls, so you say, "Save this number as Ms. Lopez." If a strange number rings, you might say, "Who is this?" or "Block it." Some people put in a birthday so the phone can remind them. If you ever cry out, "I lost all my numbers!" do not worry, because most phones keep a copy online. Parents often write the school's number on a paper and tuck it in a backpack too.

Halve it.

Mr. Okafor, a retired teacher, was washing dishes when he remembered his granddaughter's party. He dried his hands and said, "How many days until June ninth?" The assistant understood that he wanted to count the days from today to that date. It told him there were forty days left. "Plenty of time," he said. Then he asked, "If twelve children come and each one gets two cookies, how many cookies is that?" The assistant counted for him and said twenty-four. He had a free afternoon, so he decided to bake that very day. He put the big cookie jar on the table, pulled out the flour, and asked the assistant to remind him in thirty minutes to check the oven. It said it would.

Luis the cook stood at the back door of the cafe, looking sad. The box with his new oven thermometer should have come by now. "Still no sign of my package," he told the smart speaker. "It's the only meter I trust, and dinner service starts at five." The assistant understood that he wanted to know where his order was. It looked up the tracking and said the box was out for delivery and would arrive between two and four o'clock. Luis asked it to run the check again at three, and it did. At three the assistant said the driver was only two stops away. Luis smiled and went back to the stove to chop onions.

Walt was not good with technology. At breakfast he held his phone and frowned. He wanted to hear the gentle gardening podcast his neighbor liked. "Garden show," he said. The assistant understood that he meant the gardening podcast and played the newest episode. A few minutes later he said, "Slower." The assistant understood that the voices were too quick, and it set the playback speed a little slower than normal. When the postman came to the door, Walt got up and the phone went quiet. Back at the table he said, "Where was I?" The assistant picked up the episode right where he had stopped, at minute twelve, and Walt went back to his toast.

Rosa, a cook, was pushing a heavy cart of vegetables across the kitchen when she remembered her sister's birthday. It falls in November, and last year she forgot the card. "Remind me tomorrow at seven to order a cake for Mia's birthday," she said to her phone. The assistant understood that she wanted a reminder at seven o'clock the next morning about the cake. It set the reminder and read it back to her. Rosa also asked for a few gift ideas that would make Mia happy. The assistant listed a book of recipes, a nice scarf, and a small plant. Rosa liked the scarf and wrote it on her list.

A video meeting is a call where people join from different places, usually by clicking a link at the right time. It is for talking things through without travelling. Before it starts, many people read the agenda, a short list of what will be talked about. They change small things all the time. They say, "Mute me," "Share my screen," or "Move the meeting to ten." If someone joins by mistake, they say, "That was a false start, let me leave and come back." In the morning rush people also ask, "Join my next call," or "Read me the agenda." Most people just want the call to open quickly and quietly.

Tom was late. He circled the block with an egg sandwich going cold on the seat and coffee that tasted sour. "This street has no spaces, and my meeting starts in ten minutes," he said to the car assistant. The assistant understood that he needed a place to park right away. It pointed him to a garage two blocks away that still had open spaces and showed the turns on the screen. When he reached it, the assistant told him the price was three dollars an hour and asked how long he would stay. Tom said two hours, and it noted the time so it could warn him before it ran out. He made the meeting with a minute to spare.

They want the house to be warmer.
Heat up the living room.
It's freezing in here.
Set it to twenty-two.
I prefer it toasty, so bump the thermostat up by two degrees.
My feet are ice blocks.
Everyone in town says it's the coldest night of the year, so please turn the radiators up.
It's so cold that my mood has gone sour, give me more heat.
Could you please make the bedroom cozier before I get home at six?

Person: wht time is the next bus to the market
Assistant: I can look that up. Which stop will you leave from?

Gus was not good with technology, but his doctor wanted him to walk more. On a lovely morning by the river, he held up his phone and said, "Start a walking workout and keep count of my steps." The assistant understood two things at once: begin a workout timer, and count his steps. It started both and said, "Your walk has started." Gus put the phone in his pocket and strolled along the water, watching the ducks. After a while he asked, "How long have I gone?" The assistant said twenty minutes and about two thousand steps. Gus said, "Stop the workout," and the assistant stopped it and saved the walk for later.

Nora the gardener felt a sharp pain in her tooth while she was digging in the west bed. She wiped her hands on her apron and said, "Dentist tomorrow." The assistant understood that she wanted a dentist appointment for the next day. It asked what time she liked, and she answered, "Morning." The assistant checked the clinic near her house and found that Dr. Shah had a slot at nine o'clock. It booked the visit and set a reminder for eight. It also said the clinic closed at five, in case she changed her mind. Nora thanked it and went back to her roses, careful to chew on the other side that day.

Sam, an office worker, sat in a cafe near work and saw an unknown device asking to connect to his phone. "Turn off my bluetooth," he said, "and make my password longer, double what it is now." The assistant understood two things. It switched the bluetooth off, and it said his password had twelve letters, so a new one with twenty-four would be twice as long. It offered to suggest a new one, but Sam said he would type it himself. He had a bad feeling about the device and wanted to block it for good, so the assistant also told him how to forget unknown devices. Sam felt a lot safer after that.

They want a length in centimeters told to them in inches.
hw many inchs is 30 cm
30 cm in inches?
Remind me how many inches thirty centimeters is.
Quick, my hands are damp from the sink, what is 30 cm on a ruler in inches?
My tape measure only has inches and the shelf is thirty centimeters wide, what does that come to?
The planks at our village shop are sold in centimeters, but my saw is marked in inches. How long is a 30 cm plank?
Could you tell me how long thirty centimeters is in inches, please?

Ana woke up in the middle of a gray morning, rubbed her eyes, and mumbled, "I wonder if my boots ever left the warehouse." Outside, a truck rumbled along the highway and a neighbor shouted hello to someone. The assistant understood that she wanted to know the status of her boots order. It checked and told her the boots had left the warehouse yesterday and were on a truck headed her way, due on Thursday. It also said the shop had a refund option if the boots did not come by Friday. Ana pulled the blanket back over her shoulders and went back to sleep for ten more minutes.

name: robot_mower_schedule

people say:

- Skip mowing on rainy days
- Cut the lawn on weekends only

Kim, a nurse, got home after a night shift too tired to mop the kitchen floor. She sat down and said, "Delete the reminder about the old phone bill, and remind me to pay the electric one tomorrow at seven." The assistant understood that she wanted one reminder removed and a new one made. It deleted the old one, then set the electric bill reminder for seven the next morning. Kim asked for a special sound for that alert, so the assistant picked a soft bell. She smiled, said thank you, and fell asleep on the couch before the mop even came out.

A shopping list is a note of the things you need to buy. It helps you remember what ran out, so you do not walk home from the shop without the milk. People change the list all week. They say, "We are out of eggs, put them on the list," or "Take bananas off." Some ask, "What is in the fridge?" before they go. A family that likes fish from the sea might write salmon at the top. At the start of each week, many people restart the list with only the things that are running low, and they put the least urgent items at the bottom.

They want to know which bill has to be paid next.
Next bill?
What do I owe soon?

I want to buy cheese and wine for Saturday with whatever is left after paying, so what is due next?
How many days until my next payment is due?
Could you please tell me which payment I need to make first? I'm traveling south on Friday and won't have internet there.

Person: Can you make the sprinklers run more this week?
Assistant: Sure. Which ones, the front yard or the back yard?

Assistant: Sorry, I can't see the sprinklers or find a broken one. I can put it on your to-do list so you remember to check the heads.
Person: Yes, do that.

Baking turns dough or batter into bread, cakes, or cookies by heating it in the oven. The time and the heat matter a lot. Bread dough needs to rise first, which can take an hour. While it rests, some people keep the kitchen quiet and warm. They change things as they go. They say, "Bake it ten minutes longer," "Lower the oven to a hundred and eighty," or "Set a timer for the dough." In an old house the lights may dim when the oven and the blender run together, so many bakers mix first and heat later. A local bakery will often tell you the same thing: if the top gets dark too soon, cover it and turn the heat down.

A phone has a battery that runs down as you use it, a screen with a brightness you can change, and a place to keep photos called storage. People change these things all the time. They say, "Make the screen dimmer," "Turn on do not disturb," or "How much battery is left?" When a guest visits and asks for the Wi-Fi, you might hold up the phone and say, "Show the network name." If the phone says it is full, people say, "Search for my old photos," so they can delete the ones they do not need. An old phone often needs charging twice a day.

Edna was not good with technology. She sat in the mall food court with her phone and noticed a man next to her glancing at the screen. "Excuse me, could you please lock my phone? I think a stranger is looking, and I don't want him to read my messages," she said quietly. The assistant understood that she wanted the screen locked right away. It locked the phone, and a small blue padlock showed on the screen. Then it asked if she wanted to name a new passcode, and she said she would do that at home. Edna took a breath, thanked it, and finished her tea.

In an emergency, the goal is to stay safe and get help fast. A smoke alarm beeps when it senses smoke, and a power cut turns off the lights and the fridge. Many families keep a flashlight and a gallon of water for each person in a cupboard. A full jug weighs about eight pounds, so keep it somewhere easy to reach. People ask for simple things. They say, "Call for help," "Turn the alarm off," or "Is the power out on my street?" In a plain, calm voice they might also say, "Call my sister," so she knows they are safe.

Grandpa Ben had a flat tire last week, and he did not want it to happen again. "Remind me every Sunday to check my tire pressure," he told the speaker. "And keep the sound less loud than my alarm clock, it scared me last time." The assistant understood that he wanted a weekly reminder on Sundays, with a quieter sound. It set the reminder and lowered the volume to half of what it was. Ben also asked it to tell him if the pressure was ever lower than thirty-two, but the assistant said it could only remind him, not measure the tire. Ben nodded and said that was enough.

Person: Oh dear. I have letters to send and I am out of stamps.
Assistant: I can help. Do you want the nearest post office, and should I check its hours?
Person: Yes. Everyone says it closes early on Fridays.
Assistant: The one on Main Street closes at four today. It is three now. Do you want directions?
Person: Please. I need to subtract the walk from the time I have left.
Assistant: It is a twelve minute walk, so you have plenty of time.
Person: That makes me happy. Can you mail the letters for me?
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't mail things. I can give you the walking route when you are ready to leave.

They want to be told when the cookies are done.
Ten minutes.
Ping me at twelve.
Tell me when to pull the tray out.
Let me know when the oven time runs out.
Give me a quiet buzz when the cookies are golden, the baby is asleep.
Start a timer for the next step.

Ivan woke up late with his hair a mess and the fan still spinning above the bed. "Could you please tell me how much time is left on my street parking? I think I slept longer than I planned, and I don't want a ticket," he said. The assistant understood that he wanted to know the time left on his parking spot. It said there were twelve minutes left. Ivan asked, "Is it true that parking is free after nine?" The assistant said that was true on his street. He decided to wash his face first, then pulled on his shoes and hurried down to move the car.

A to-do list is a place to keep the jobs you want to finish. Each task is one line, and you check it off when it is done, which feels good. Some jobs matter more, so people mark them as first. They change the list a lot. They say, "Put call the bank on my list," "Check off the laundry," or "Move dentist to the top." Small tasks can be simple, like emptying the dishwasher or heating lunch in the microwave. Some people write one healthy goal each day, like a walk. At night they ask, "What is left?" to see what to do tomorrow.

Assistant: The photo is taken and saved to the Family album.

Assistant: Sorry, I can't edit photos. I can open the picture so you can use an editing app.
Person: Okay, open it please.

Taking medicine means following a dose, which says how much to take and how often. A daily pill is easy to forget, so many people use a reminder. They ask for small changes, such as, "Remind me to take my pill at eight," "Move my doctor visit to Friday," or "Pull up my appointment." When a symptom shows up, like a cough, people write it on a page in a notebook to tell the doctor later. A pharmacist can answer questions about doses, and a doctor decides any change to them.

Marta strapped the bikes to the roof of the car and loaded the kids in. "Plan a ride north along the river," she said to her phone, "but not on the main road, and no big hills." The assistant understood that she wanted a flat bike route heading north that avoided the main road. It said it had found a path eleven kilometers long, mostly flat, with a park halfway where the children could rest. Marta asked it to say the turns out loud while she drove to the start. The assistant said it would. At the park the kids ate snacks, and then they rode back along the same path.

Translating means saying the same thing in another language. Travelers use it a lot. At a market, someone who wants to buy bread might say, "How do I say two loaves, please?" People also learn phrases for hello, thank you, and where is the station. A lesson can be short, even five minutes a day. A thin pocket dictionary used to be the usual tool, but now people ask their phone. They say, "Translate this into Spanish," "How do you spell that?" or "Say it again slowly."

Leo, a student, was hot from the heat of the afternoon and wanted dinner with friends. "Find a place with half-price burgers," he said, "and less than twenty minutes by public bus." The assistant understood that he wanted a cheap burger restaurant reachable by bus in under twenty minutes. It found the Blue Cow Diner, which had half-price burgers on Tuesdays and was a fifteen-minute ride away. It said the place was open until ten. Leo asked it to book a table for four at seven, and it did. He sent the news to his friends and went to find his bus pass.

Reply when the machine is running at full power.
Please turn on the air machine in the bedroom, because I just used strong glue on a model plane and the smell is bothering me.

Hana woke up with the sun in her eyes and croaked, "Find the last episode I heard, the one about poetry meter." The assistant understood that she wanted the podcast episode she had been listening to the night before. It found the show and started it at the place she had stopped, a little past minute forty. Hana mumbled, "Go back twenty seconds." The assistant jumped back and played that part again. She lay there listening while the coffee machine hissed in the kitchen. After a few minutes she asked for the next episode, and the assistant queued it up for her.

A television shows channels, and many also stream shows through the internet. The remote changes the channel, the volume, and the subtitles. People change things all the time. They say, "Put on the news," "Turn the subtitles on," "Make it louder," or "Remove that channel from my favorites." On a holiday, a whole family might gather and say, "What's on tonight?" A polite guest may ask, "May I change the channel?" before picking up the remote. If the show is too late, people say, "Record it for tomorrow," or "Stop in an hour."

They want to know how many centimeters are in one inch.
How many cm in an inch?
inch to cm

Tell me how long an inch is in centimeters.

How big is one inch if I measure in centimeters?
Could you please tell me how many centimeters make up one inch? My phone battery is almost dead, and I have to drop my sizes off at the local shop before it closes.

An air conditioner keeps a room cool when the weather is hot. People mostly change three things: the temperature, the fan speed and the timer. To make a room cooler they say, make it colder, or, set it to twenty degrees. If the air feels too strong they say, turn the fan down. Some people divide the day in two, with a cool bedroom at night and a warmer house while they are out. A pale curtain helps keep the sun out, and a cold room feels like the inside of a fridge where a potato stays fresh. To stop the cooling, people say, switch it off, or, turn the cooling off at ten.

A smart lock opens and closes a front door without a key. It is for safety, and for letting the right people in. People change who can come in, when the door locks by itself, and whether it is locked right now. They say, lock the front door, is the door locked, or, let the dog walker in until five. A polite visitor rings the bell, and a small camera shows who is there. If you wish to stop a guest from coming in, you ask the assistant to take away their code. A lost key can mean a trip to the shop for a refund or a new copy, but a lost code is easy: you just ask for a new one.

Rosa was making soup when she saw that the kitchen bin was full. She spoke to her phone. "Could you please tell me when the recycling truck comes? I would like to put the bins out in good time, because last week I missed it and the boxes piled up in the hall." The assistant looked up her street and said the truck comes on Thursday morning, which was tomorrow. Rosa then asked it to explain what goes in the green bin. The assistant said clean glass, cans and paper go in the green bin, and food scraps go in the compost. It also set a reminder for Wednesday at eight in the evening. Last, it told her the recycling center is a mile from her house, for anything too big for the bin.

A focus timer helps you work for a short time and then rest. A common plan is twenty-five minutes of work and then five minutes of break. People use it when they have a whole pile of jobs and cannot decide where to start. They change the length of the work time, the length of the break and the number of rounds. They say, set a timer for twenty minutes, make my breaks longer, or, start another round. A break is for standing up, drinking water and letting your eyes look at something far away. If you have a cough or feel tired, you might say, stop the timer and end the day early.

Mina was ten years old and hungry after school. Her mom was still at work, so Mina spoke to the tablet in the kitchen. "Please, could you order a cheese pizza from Tony's? My mom said it is fine, and my friend Sam is a student at the high school who is coming to help me with homework, so we need enough for two." The assistant said it understood: one large cheese pizza from Tony's, to be delivered to her address. It said her mom would have to say yes to the payment first. Mina asked it to switch the order to two small pizzas, and the assistant changed it. It told her delivery would take about thirty minutes, and it sent a message to her mom asking her to approve the order.

Dan was pouring cereal for the kids when he remembered the Sunday ride. "Find me a flat bike route by the river and tell me how far it is," he said to his phone. The assistant found a loop along the river path and said it is eighteen kilometers long. Dan said it sounded good, and the assistant saved the route and tagged it family ride. Then he asked about a new bike light, but the first ones he saw were pricey, so he told the assistant to forget it for now. The assistant dropped the search. It also set a reminder for Saturday night to charge the bike lights, so the kids would be ready in the morning.

I hate to be rude, but yogurt got stuck in the pump and the machine has not worked for twenty-five days, so I would like the first visit you can find.

Person: No, thank you. This is enough.

The inbox is where new email arrives. It is for reading messages, writing back and keeping the letters you need. People change what they see: only unread mail, mail from one person, or mail with an attachment. They say, show my unread mail, find the email from Sam, or, write back and say I'll know by Friday. A photo of your garden can be an attachment, but a huge file may be too big to send, so people ask to make it smaller first. When mail piles up they say, delete the old ones, or, mark everything as read.

Mr. Alvarez, a retired teacher, stood on the sand with his phone in a plastic bag. It was early and the sea looked cold. "How warm is the water today? Is it warmer than yesterday?" he asked. The assistant said the water was eighteen degrees, which is two degrees warmer than yesterday. Then he asked how often he should put on sun cream, and the assistant said every two hours, and twice as often after swimming. The waves were loud, so he turned up the speaker on his phone. Last, he asked the assistant to call his wife and say he would swim for half an hour. The assistant made the call and left the message.

name: play_voicemail
does: Plays the voice messages people left on your phone, newest first, and says who called and when, so you are ready to call back.
inputs: which messages you want (new or all), and a caller's name if you only want one person
people say:

- I'm getting ready to ride my motorcycle, did anyone leave a message
- who called while I was out
- let me hear what mom said

Priya came home after a night shift, too tired to hurry. She leaned on the door and asked her phone, "Could you please check if my parcel has come? I am waiting for my medicine, and I am too tired to walk down to the mailbox if it is not there yet." The assistant looked at the tracking page and said the parcel had been left in the mailbox at nine that morning. It said the parcel was a thick envelope and that no signature was needed. Priya thanked it, and the assistant also set a reminder for four in the afternoon, to take the medicine with food.

Omar was putting on his coat. He had no time to fry eggs that morning, and the dog sat by the door looking bored. "Turn the alarm on, but don't turn off the hallway camera," he said to the speaker. "And I don't want the porch light on, it's daytime." The assistant said it understood: the alarm was on, the hallway camera was still recording, and the porch light stayed off. It also said the front door was locked. Omar asked about the spare key under the stone by the gate, but the assistant said it could not see that. Omar laughed, picked up his bag and ran for the bus.

A video meeting lets people who are in different places talk together. It is for planning, sharing news and getting work done. Before it starts, someone writes an agenda, which is a short list of what to talk about. A shared screen lets everyone see the same thing, like a plain list or a picture of a bike wheel. People change who can talk, whether the camera is on, and what is shown on the screen. They say, join my two o'clock call, share my screen, mute me, or, fill in the agenda with the budget. When the meeting is over they say, leave the call.

A score keeper helps players of a board game or card game remember who is winning. Games have rules, and a timer can show how long each turn takes. People change the number of players, the time on the clock and the points they give. They say, start a game for four, set the timer to one minute, give Ana five points, or, whose turn is it. In a farm card game, a milk card might be worth three points. In a shop game, a player can charge another player rent. When the game is over, people ask, who got the right answers, or, read me the final scores.

Assistant: Happy to do both. Which story, and how long should the lights stay dim?
Person: The bear one. Half an hour. I have to go and grill the fish.
